statement: Lily colours every whole number on a number line from 6 to 14, including 6 and 14. How many numbers does she colour?

choices.misconception: I left out 6 and 14, but the question says they are included.
I took 6 away from 14, which counts the jumps between the numbers, not the numbers.
I gave the last number she colours instead of how many numbers she colours.
I added 6 and 14 instead of counting the numbers from one to the other.

hints: Write the numbers out. Does 6 belong in your list?
Make a list that starts at 6 and stops at 14, because both ends are included. Writing the list is safer than subtracting, because subtracting counts the jumps and is easy to get one off.
The list is 6, 7, 8 and so on, up to 14. Write every number and count them.

solutions.reliable: Both ends are included, so the list starts at 6 and stops at 14: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. That is 9 numbers. The idea to keep: when you count the numbers from one to another, check whether the two ends belong in your list.
solutions.elegant: From 6 to 14 is 14 take away 6, which is 8 jumps. Each jump lands on a new number, and the starting number 6 is coloured too, so 8 + 1 = 9. The idea to keep: counting both ends gives one more number than there are jumps.

whyOnTest: Counting the numbers from one point to another on a number line tests whether the ends belong, the classic off-by-one trap.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
